articles.label: ACCOUNTABILITY
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2M Tourism Contract Renewed Without Public Bid
articles.dek: The county commission quietly extended its marketing deal with a Tallahassee firm last week. Three commissioners have received campaign contributions from the company's lobbyist.
brief: Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 to renew a $4.2 million tourism marketing contract with Visit Florida Partners without soliciting competitive bids.
Campaign finance records show three commissioners who voted yes received a combined $14,500 from the firm's registered lobbyist since 2024.
The lone dissenting vote came from Commissioner Janet Underwood, who called the process 'a disservice to taxpayers.'
articles.body:
The agenda item appeared on page 47 of the consent calendar. No discussion. No public comment. The Escambia County Commission approved a three-year, $4.2 million contract renewal for tourism marketing services in under ninety seconds last Thursday.

Visit Florida Partners, a Tallahassee-based marketing firm, has held the county's tourism promotion contract since 2019. The renewal extends that relationship through 2029 without the county soliciting proposals from competing firms.

County Administrator Wes Moreno told The Flightline the decision followed standard procurement procedures. "The contract includes renewal options that were negotiated in the original agreement," Moreno said in an email. "This is consistent with how we handle ongoing service contracts."

But campaign finance records reviewed by The Flightline show a financial connection between the firm and the commissioners who approved the deal.

The Money Trail

Marcus Webb has served as Visit Florida Partners' registered lobbyist in Escambia County since 2021, according to filings with the county clerk's office. During that time, Webb has contributed $14,500 to three sitting commissioners through his political committee, Gulf Coast Leadership PAC.

Commissioner Doug Bergosh received $6,000 across four contributions since January 2024. Commissioner Mike Kohler received $5,000. Commissioner Steven Barry received $3,500.

All three voted yes on Thursday's renewal.

Webb did not respond to phone and email requests for comment. Bergosh, reached by phone Friday, said the contributions had no bearing on his vote.

"Marcus supports a lot of candidates," Bergosh said. "I've known him for years. That has nothing to do with how I vote on contracts."

Kohler and Barry did not respond to requests for comment.

'Why Aren't We Looking Around?'

Commissioner Janet Underwood cast the only vote against the renewal. She asked for the item to be pulled from the consent agenda for discussion, but the motion failed 4-1.

"Four point two million dollars is not a small number," Underwood said after the meeting. "At a minimum, we should be asking: Is this still the best deal? Are there other firms who could do this work? Why aren't we looking around?"

Underwood said she was not alleging any improper behavior but called the process "a disservice to taxpayers who expect us to be careful with their money."

Florida law does not require competitive bidding for professional services contracts, leaving the decision to individual governments. Escambia County's procurement policy allows contract renewals when "continuation of services is in the best interest of the county," according to the county code.

Moreno said the tourism contract met that standard based on performance metrics. Visit Florida Partners reported a 12% increase in website traffic to VisitPensacola.com last year and coordinated marketing campaigns that reached an estimated 45 million impressions, according to documents included in the agenda packet.

What the Contract Covers

The $4.2 million over three years breaks down to roughly $1.4 million annually. The contract covers digital advertising, social media management, travel writer outreach, trade show representation, and creative services for the county's tourism division.

Funding comes from the county's share of the local tourist development tax—the so-called bed tax collected on short-term rentals and hotel stays. That revenue stream generated $18.7 million for Escambia County in fiscal year 2025, according to the tax collector's office.

Visit Florida Partners is one of several firms that specialize in destination marketing for Florida counties. Competitors include Paradise Advertising based in St. Petersburg and Beaches & Beyond Marketing in Fort Lauderdale. Neither firm was contacted about the Escambia contract, county records show.

The Flightline submitted a public records request Friday for all communications between county staff and Visit Florida Partners regarding the contract renewal. The county has 10 business days to respond under Florida law.

A Pattern?

This is not the first time Escambia County has drawn scrutiny for no-bid contract extensions. In 2023, the commission renewed a $2.8 million solid waste consulting contract without competitive bidding, prompting criticism from a local taxpayer watchdog group.

That contract was later rebid after public pressure. The original firm won again—but at a rate $340,000 lower than the renewal terms.

Underwood referenced that episode Thursday. "We've seen before what happens when we actually put these things out to bid," she said. "Sometimes we save money. Sometimes we find out we were getting a good deal. Either way, the public deserves to know."

The tourism contract takes effect October 1.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Pensacola Beach Parking Garage Proposal Returns—This Time With Hotel Attached
articles.dek: Santa Rosa Island Authority will hear a revised pitch Tuesday for a 400-space structure near Casino Beach. Residents who killed the last version say they weren't notified.
brief: Developer Innisfree Hotels will present plans for a 400-space parking garage with 120-room hotel at Tuesday's SRIA meeting
The previous standalone garage proposal died in 2023 after residents packed a public hearing to oppose it
Critics say the revised project wasn't properly noticed and circumvents the public input that stopped it before
articles.body:
The parking lot at Via de Luna and Fort Pickens Road fills by 10 a.m. most summer Saturdays. By noon, cars circle the blocks near Casino Beach like vultures, waiting for someone to leave. The overflow spills onto side streets, into the lots of businesses that post tow-away signs they rarely enforce.

This is the problem everyone on Pensacola Beach agrees exists. What they cannot agree on is the solution.

On Tuesday evening, the Santa Rosa Island Authority will hear a proposal that its backers say solves the parking crisis while generating lease revenue for the beach. Innisfree Hotels, the Pensacola-based company that operates the Hampton Inn and Hilton Garden Inn on the beach, wants to build a 400-space parking garage on SRIA-controlled land one block north of the Casino Beach parking lot. Attached to it: a 120-room boutique hotel.

The hotel component is new. The parking garage is not.

A Proposal Resurrected

In September 2023, a different developer brought a standalone parking structure to the SRIA board. That proposal called for 350 spaces on a smaller footprint, with ground-floor retail. It never made it to a formal vote.

More than 80 residents packed the SRIA meeting room that night. They questioned the traffic impact on Via de Luna. They challenged the developer's revenue projections. They asked why public land should be leased for private profit when the county could build and operate its own structure.

The board tabled the item indefinitely. The developer withdrew weeks later.

Now a new proposal has appeared on Tuesday's agenda, and some of the same residents who organized against the first one say they learned about it through an automated calendar alert—not through any official notice.

"I found out because I subscribe to the SRIA meeting feed," said Deborah Kessler, who lives on Ariola Drive and spoke against the 2023 proposal. "Nobody called. Nobody sent a mailer. There was no community meeting."

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio said the authority followed its standard notification procedures. Agenda items are posted to the SRIA website seven days before meetings. Adjacent leaseholders within 300 feet received mailed notice, as required by SRIA development review rules.

"This is a conceptual presentation," Ghio said. "No vote is scheduled. If the board wants to move forward, there would be additional public hearings before any lease agreement."

What the Proposal Includes

According to documents submitted to the SRIA and obtained by The Flightline, Innisfree proposes a five-story structure on the 1.2-acre parcel currently used as an overflow lot during peak season. The first two floors would contain 400 parking spaces available to the public. Floors three through five would house the hotel, with rooms facing the Santa Rosa Sound rather than the Gulf.

Innisfree would pay the SRIA an annual base lease of $180,000, plus 3% of gross parking revenue and 2% of gross hotel revenue. The company estimates the combined payments would exceed $300,000 annually by year five of operations.

The public parking spaces would be managed by the SRIA's existing contractor, Premium Parking, under the same rate structure as the Casino Beach lot. Currently that means $5 per hour or $20 per day during peak season, free for Santa Rosa County residents with a beach parking pass.

Innisfree CEO John Greene did not respond to requests for comment. A company spokesperson confirmed the Tuesday presentation but declined to discuss specifics before the meeting.

'Different Project, Same Problems'

Terry Rowan has owned a beach house on Ensenada Marbella since 2004. He was among the most vocal opponents of the 2023 proposal and said the new version raises the same concerns—plus new ones.

"Now you're not just talking about a parking garage. You're talking about a hotel that will generate its own traffic, its own demand for parking, its own strain on Via de Luna," Rowan said. "And they want to use public land to do it."

The parcel in question is part of the SRIA's leasehold from Escambia County. Like all developed land on Pensacola Beach, it is technically owned by the county and leased through the SRIA, which manages the beach's infrastructure and development. Lease terms for commercial properties typically run 30 to 50 years.

Rowan and other critics argue that a publicly controlled parking structure—built with bonds or tourism tax revenue—would serve the same purpose without enriching a private developer.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he has not taken a position on the proposal but believes the conversation is worth having.

"Parking at the beach is a real issue, and it's only getting worse," Bergosh said. "I don't know if this is the right answer. But I want to hear what they're proposing and what the residents think."

Traffic and Timing

A traffic study submitted with the Innisfree proposal estimates the combined garage and hotel would generate approximately 1,100 additional vehicle trips per day during peak season. The study, conducted by Kimley-Horn, concludes that existing infrastructure can accommodate the increase with minor signal timing adjustments at Via de Luna and Fort Pickens Road.

Kessler, the Ariola Drive resident, called that conclusion "fantasy."

"Anyone who has sat in the backup trying to get off the beach on a Sunday afternoon knows that intersection is already failing," she said. "You cannot add 1,100 cars and call it minor."

The proposal does not include any road improvements. Ghio said such requirements would be determined during the formal site plan review process, if the board directs staff to proceed.

Tuesday's meeting begins at 5 p.m. at the SRIA office, 1 Via de Luna Drive. Public comment is scheduled for after the Innisfree presentation.

Kessler said she will be there. So will Rowan. They have been texting other residents who showed up in 2023.

"They're hoping nobody notices," Kessler said. "We noticed."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors and a Reckoning for Beach Road Traffic
articles.dek: With the July show two months out, county officials admit they still haven't finalized a plan for Via de Luna gridlock that stranded thousands last year.
brief: Escambia County officials expect 200,000 visitors for the July Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show but have not finalized traffic management plans for Via de Luna Drive
Last year's show left thousands stranded on Pensacola Beach for up to five hours as a single-road evacuation created miles-long gridlock
County commissioners will hold an emergency planning session June 3 after beachside business owners demanded answers at this week's public meeting
articles.body:
The line of brake lights stretched from the Portofino towers to the Bob Sikes Bridge and beyond. Parents rationed water bottles. Toddlers melted down in car seats. Some families gave up entirely, parking in restaurant lots and walking to the Sandshaker to wait out the gridlock with a bushwacker.

That was July 12, 2025. The Blue Angels had put on a flawless 45-minute show over Pensacola Beach. What followed was a five-hour exodus that left an estimated 8,000 vehicles crawling down Via de Luna Drive at walking speed.

Now, with the 2026 Homecoming Air Show scheduled for July 11, Escambia County officials acknowledge they still don't have a finalized plan to prevent a repeat.

"We're working on it," Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said at Tuesday's commission meeting. "We've had conversations with the Sheriff's Office, with the Navy, with FDOT. But I can't sit here today and tell you we've got it solved."

A Single Road, 200,000 People

The math is brutal. Via de Luna Drive is the only road connecting Pensacola Beach to the mainland. It feeds into a two-lane bridge. On a normal summer Saturday, beach traffic can back up for 30 minutes. During the air show, when the Navy estimates 200,000 spectators pack the beach and surrounding areas, that single artery becomes a tourniquet.

Last year's gridlock prompted a flood of complaints to county offices and a viral Facebook post from a Panama City family who documented their 4.5-hour crawl in real time. The post was shared more than 3,000 times.

"We've been coming to this show for 15 years," wrote Jamie Thornton, the post's author. "Never again. Not unless they figure out how to get people home."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which manages beach infrastructure, has limited tools. SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio told The Flightline the authority can adjust parking and coordinate with vendors but has no control over traffic flow on county and state roads.

"We can encourage staggered departures. We can ask people to stay and enjoy the beach after the show," Ghio said. "But we can't make them."

Business Owners Demand Answers

At Tuesday's commission meeting, a half-dozen Pensacola Beach business owners lined up during public comment to press for details.

Danny Strickland, who owns the Gulf Breeze-based charter company Coastal Expeditions, said he lost an estimated $4,000 in afternoon bookings last year when clients couldn't reach his dock.

"The show ends at 3 p.m. My 4 o'clock fishing trip doesn't leave until 8:30 because nobody can get there," Strickland said. "That's not a traffic jam. That's a failure."

Maureen LaSalle, general manager of a Via de Luna restaurant she asked not to be named for fear of Navy blowback, said the gridlock created a different problem: customers who couldn't leave.

"We had people sitting at tables for three hours after they paid their checks," LaSalle said. "They were lovely about it. But my staff couldn't turn tables. We lost a dinner service."

Commissioner Bergosh announced at the meeting's end that the board would hold an emergency planning session June 3 with representatives from the Escambia County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Transportation, the Navy, and SRIA.

Options Under Consideration

County staff have floated several potential measures, though none have been approved:

Staggered show times. The Navy has historically resisted splitting the demonstration into multiple performances, citing fuel costs and pilot schedules. A county request to explore this option is pending with NAS Pensacola public affairs.

Remote parking with shuttle service. FDOT has identified potential staging areas at Pensacola State College's Warrington campus and the former Cordova Mall overflow lot. Shuttle logistics and costs have not been determined.

Contraflow on the Bob Sikes Bridge. Converting both lanes to outbound traffic after the show would require FDOT approval, law enforcement staffing, and coordination with Gulf Breeze emergency services. A 2019 feasibility study found the approach "viable but complex."

Enhanced real-time communication. The county is exploring a text-alert system that would notify spectators when traffic has cleared to safe levels. Opt-in sign-ups would be promoted in advance.

Sheriff Chip Simmons, whose deputies manage beach traffic, said at a separate press availability Thursday that his office is prepared to implement whatever plan the county approves.

"We'll put bodies where they tell us to put bodies," Simmons said. "But somebody's got to make the call on what we're actually doing."

The Navy's Position

NAS Pensacola Public Affairs Officer Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Torres said in an emailed statement that the Navy "values its partnership with Escambia County and the Pensacola Beach community" and is "committed to working collaboratively on traffic management solutions."

The statement did not address specific proposals or whether the Navy would consider format changes to the show.

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show is the squadron's only home performance each year and routinely draws the largest single-day crowd of any event in Northwest Florida. The Navy considers it a premier recruiting opportunity and community relations event.

"We understand the traffic challenges are significant," Torres's statement continued. "We encourage spectators to plan ahead, arrive early, and consider staying on the beach after the demonstration concludes."

Two Months and Counting

The June 3 planning session is open to the public and will be held at the Escambia County Central Office Complex on Palafox Street at 9 a.m.

Commissioner Lumon May, whose district includes much of the beach access corridor, said he would push for a concrete commitment before the meeting adjourns.

"Last year was embarrassing," May said. "We had families with small children stuck in cars in July heat. We had medical calls for dehydration. We cannot wing this again."

The 2026 show is scheduled for Saturday, July 11, with a practice demonstration Friday, July 10. Gates open at 8 a.m. The Blue Angels are slated to fly at 2 p.m.

For Jamie Thornton, the Panama City visitor whose viral post captured last year's frustration, the county's response so far hasn't changed her mind.

"Call me when they figure it out," she said in a phone interview this week. "Until then, we'll watch from our backyard. The jets fly right over us anyway."
